description: STRONG-ADMISSION VOCABULARY, WEAK EVIDENCE: the four arms of the twelve that measurement did not support — `(fail*|unable|inabilit*|attempt*) to replicate`, `(aim*|set out) to replicate`, `success* replicat*` and the negation matrix — carried anywhere in title-or-abstract. They are held in their own tier because they are the measured problem cases, not because they are a different kind of claim: each of them reads as a paper saying it did a replication, and each of them is also the ordinary way to write a sentence ABOUT one. Measured MARGINALLY — over the rows no other arm of the twelve reached — their FLoRA yields are 2.9, 2.3, 2.5 and 0.66 papers per thousand exclusive pool rows, against 24, 15 and 14 for the best of the eight strong arms, and their cached two-voter screen precisions on that same slice are 35%, 42%, 13% and 10%. An order of magnitude on yield is not a tuning difference. One clause per arm, so each arm can be measured and retired on its own evidence — the engine attributes a hit to the rule, not the arm, so an arm's count is a separate evaluation of that arm's pattern. Every regex is carried verbatim from the twelve-arm `replication-claim` this family replaces. Note what is NOT in any arm. Bare `replications? of` is deliberately excluded: it is the highest-recall phrase in the book (40.4% of positives) and also fires on 82.2% of screen-confirmed negatives, and no cheap syntactic anchor repairs it — it is `replication-signal`'s last arm instead. `registered report of` is excluded because most Registered Reports are original studies. Reproduction vocabulary is out of scope entirely; it belongs to `reproduction-signal` and #155. Every tier of this family routes to the same pile, so precedence here decides ATTRIBUTION, not destination: which tier `filter_evidence` records for a row several tiers claim, and therefore the order a worklist can be worked in. The ordering is by measured specificity — cited-title (760), title (750), text (730), residual (710) — so a row is credited to the narrowest claim that reaches it. The whole family sits in the 700s strong-admission band for the reason the single rule did: it yields to the identifier/title/type discards above it (940–960), which say the record is not a paper at all, and it outranks `not-a-study-type` (500), whose claim is a fallible registry crosswalk — so a replication mistyped as `paratext` is screened rather than deleted. It sits at the foot of the family, below `replication-claim-text` (730), so that a row reaching a strong arm as well is never credited to this one and this tier's attributed rows are exactly the rows nothing better reached. `vocabulary` stays null across the family: an admission to the two-voter screen is a request for attention, not a verdict about what the row is (CONVENTIONS.md, "Pile → paper_type"). OPEN QUESTION, and the reason this tier exists as a tier: this is where a negation or a narrowing may genuinely be needed before the arms can be admitted at all. `success* replicat*` at 13% and the negation matrix at 10% are not admissions anyone would write down as they stand — "the effect did not replicate" is written by the paper that failed to replicate it and by the review discussing that paper, and nothing in the arm separates them. What that narrowing should be is UNRESOLVED; no candidate has been measured, and one is deliberately not invented here. The arms are individually measured, so the question can be asked one arm at a time. OPEN SCOPE QUESTION (D3) lands here too: if a planned-but-not-completed replication is not a FLoRA record, the `aim|set out to replicate` arm is not an admission arm anywhere.

measured.sample: 2,895 distinct replication studies with a usable abstract from `data/FLoRA entry sheet - replication list.csv` (3,851 rows, 2,978 distinct doi_r), text = ref_r + abstract_r as a proxy for the pool row's title + abstract; scored against 501 rows of `data/not_a_replication.csv`, papers that passed the old filter, reached the two-voter screen and were judged not_a_replication. Computed 2026-08-04, proposal SS1 (redesign/rulebook_v2.html).
measured.rationale: With all twelve arms this rule fires on 82.6% of the positives at 6.8% of the false-positive load (80.8% / 6.2% without the four marginal arms). READ BOTH DENOMINATORS AS WHAT THEY ARE. The recall figure is an UPPER BOUND: a substantial share of the entry sheet was discovered by keyword search, so a phrase rule scored against it over-estimates recall, most for the arms that did the finding; the sheet's columns do not separate curated-list entries from pipeline-found ones, so this is corrected by the SS6 holdout design, not here. The 6.8% is NOT a population false-positive rate and must never be quoted as this rule's precision: the negatives corpus is the false-positive load itself — what the old loose filter admitted and the screen then rejected — so what it measures exactly is the composition of the money currently being wasted. Per-arm firing on the 501 negatives: `we replicat*` 1.6%, `replicate and extend` 1.6%, `replication study` 0.8%, `fail/attempt to replicate` 0.8%, `study replicated` 0.0%, the qualifier family 2.8%. The four marginal arms were measured MARGINALLY, i.e. what each adds once the arms above it are in: `success* replicat*` +26 positives / +2 negatives (13:1, and the only arm carrying the successful-outcome framing); the negation matrix +18 / +1; `replication attempt(s)` +8 / +0; the failure nouns +1 / +0. That last +1 is the clearest case on the page of why a marginal count is not a coverage argument: 'We present a failed replication of Smith (2009)' fires the noun arm and NOTHING ELSE in this rule, because 'replication' there is a noun and the sentence never uses the verb. It scores +1 only because in this keyword-assembled corpus the papers phrasing it that way almost all also say 'replication study' or 'we replicated' somewhere in the same abstract. A marginal count of +1 on a biased corpus is weak evidence of redundancy; a marginal count of +0 negatives is strong evidence of harmlessness, and when an arm is free the second number decides. The rule discards nothing — it admits into a tier that decides — so the evidence gate does not bind it; this entry documents the claim rather than satisfying a gate.

measured.sample: Per-arm FLoRA yield over the routed pool at release ec9497102a7e (5,146,160 rows), FLoRA-exclusive papers per 1,000 exclusive pool rows, against data/flora.csv; per-arm precision over the largest cached two-voter cohort in cache/llm/classify_*.json (n=3,000, template b4ebd5847e95, voters gemini-3.5-flash-lite+gpt-5.4-mini), on the same exclusive slice. Both are `python -m analysis.arm_evidence` outputs. READ THE DENOMINATOR: EXCLUSIVE here means exclusive against ALL TWELVE arms of the `replication-claim` this family replaces, which is the run these numbers come from (`--spec` on the twelve-arm rule). Running the same tool on THIS four-arm spec computes exclusivity against the other three arms only, and so returns much larger exclusive slices and higher yields (11.75 / 7.76 / 9.44 / 3.41) for the same four patterns. The twelve-arm figures are the ones that answer the question the split was made to ask: what does an arm add that the strong arms did not already reach.
measured.rationale: The four arms measure 2.9 / 2.3 / 2.5 / 0.66 FLoRA papers per thousand exclusive pool rows and 35% / 42% / 13% / 10% cached screen precision, in the arm order of this rule's `any_of`. The best strong arms measure 24 / 15 / 14 on the same yield scale. The cached precisions are optimistic in the way every number from that cache is — the cohort is drawn from what the OLD filter admitted — which makes the comparison between arms the usable part and the levels themselves an upper bound. The rule admits rather than discards, so the evidence gate does not bind it; this entry records why the arms are held apart.
